blocks.text: Acts 12:20-23 and Josephus independently describe Herod Agrippa I’s public death. Both accounts include royal acclaim, but they differ in their theological and medical details. The comparison is therefore suggestive rather than identical: it places Acts’ account alongside another narrative of the same public event while preserving the distinctive way Acts tells it.

sections.title: A Parallel Account of Herod’s Death

blocks.text: Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek manuscripts, whose surviving portions and textual profiles differ. Codex Bezae and related versions preserve a notably distinctive form of Acts, often called the Western text; particular differences must be assessed individually rather than assumed to be either uniformly reliable or uniformly unreliable. The same case-by-case care applies when evaluating Acts historically: individual claims are compared with independent evidence rather than assigned blanket reliability or unreliability.
